title: QGIS Handbook
text:
Introduction
A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a powerful way to work with information that’s tied to locations on Earth. This type of information, often called geospatial data, includes anything that has a geographic reference, such as coordinates, addresses, or map features. GIS allows you to store, view, analyse, and present these data so you can understand spatial patterns and relationships.
In this course, you will learn how to use GIS to solve a real-world problem: deciding where to build a wind farm. Through a series of practical exercises, you will bring together many different datasets, including land use, protected areas, topography, and average wind speed, to identify the most suitable location for a new wind farm in part of the Welsh landscape.
By the end of the course, you will be able to:

Load, explore, and manage different types of geospatial data.
Create maps and visualisations using QGIS.
Analyse spatial data to assess suitability for development.
Apply common planning and environmental constraints to real-world scenarios.

The skills you gain here can also be applied to a wide range of other questions, from identifying flood risk zones to planning urban transport routes or mapping wildlife habitats — anywhere location matters.

title: Before you begin
text:
Accessing QGIS
This chapter will help you build practical skills, avoid common pitfalls, and make the most of your time in the computer lab. You can work at your own pace, but it is important to attend all scheduled computer practicals. These sessions are your chance to share your progress, ask questions, and clear up misunderstandings in a supportive, flipped-learning environment (Dikilitas and Fructuoso 2023). By the end of this chapter, you’ll be better prepared to complete the exercises efficiently and confidently.
There are a number of ways to access QGIS:

title: Before you begin
text:
University computerPersonal computer


QGIS can be accessed from any computer around campus:

Use the ZenWorks window to navigate to Science → Geography
Double-click the QGIS icon



QGIS is free, open-source software available for Windows, Mac, and Linux. This means you’re not limited to using University computers. You can install it on your own machine and work wherever and whenever you like:

Download and install QGIS here
Double-click on the downloaded folder to start the installation. For Mac users, right-click on the folder and click Open to start the installation







Tip



I recommend installing the Long Term Release version of QGIS which, in theory, has fewer bugs in it. Download Latest Release for the most up-to-date features.

title: Before you begin
text:
Accessing the data

Navigate to the folder on OneDrive where the data is stored here
Click the Sync icon







You may need to wait a minute, but eventually the folder should be accessible via your browser

title: Before you begin
text:
Data storage
Swansea University provides secure storage through OneDrive and network drives. These appear the same no matter which University computer you log into, and you can also access OneDrive from your own devices. I have two key tips for you:

Always save your work to OneDrive. This keeps it safe from accidental loss and accessible wherever you are. Avoid storing coursework on the local C: drive. Files saved there are only available on that one machine and may be deleted automatically overnight.
Be organised. Create a clear folder structure for your GIS work and name files logically. GIS projects can generate hundreds of files. Staying tidy will save you time and frustration later.

title: Before you begin
text:
Watch your storage space
If your disk space becomes full, QGIS and other software can crash. To remedy this:

Check available space by right-clicking your OneDrive network in Windows Explorer and clicking Properties
Delete temporary or unwanted files to free up space

If problems persist (e.g. you can’t log in, access software, or save files), make a Service Centre request here.

title: Before you begin
text:
GIS software options
Two software applications presently dominate the GIS market, each with benefits and drawbacks:

ESRI ArcGIS Pro. ArcGIS Pro has been the industry leader for decades and is widely used by professionals.


Pros: Well established, feature-rich, and supported by extensive online documentation. Cons: Software is licensed and expensive.


QGIS (Quantum GIS). QGIS is an open-source application that has grown rapidly in popularity, especially in the public sector.


Pros: Free to install, open source, and increasingly competitive with ArcGIS. Cons: Still lacks some advanced functions and may be less common in certain job markets.

As a Geography Department, we’ve chosen to teach you QGIS. Why? Because it combines the power and flexibility of professional GIS with the accessibility and freedom of open-source software.
QGIS is free to install on your own computer, meaning you can practise and experiment anywhere, anytime, without relying on campus labs or expensive licences. It has a clean, intuitive interface that many beginners find easier to learn than ArcGIS, yet it still offers advanced tools used by professionals around the world.
Beyond the classroom, QGIS is rapidly gaining ground in government, consultancy, and research sectors, particularly where budgets are tight and data-sharing is important (Graser et al. 2025). Its open-source nature means new features and plugins are added by a global community of GIS experts. You’re therefore learning with a platform that’s evolving at the cutting edge.
Mastering QGIS now gives you a career-ready skillset, the ability to collaborate internationally without licence barriers, and the confidence that you can always access a powerful GIS toolkit long after graduation.

title: Before you begin
text:
Developing your computer skills
The most effective way to learn GIS is to use it. The practical exercises are designed to guide you through the most common functions in QGIS, helping you build skills and create results you can use in your coursework, projects, or dissertation.
Here are my protips for learning QGIS:

Expect to make mistakes and repeat steps. This repetition will help you remember processes. QGIS can occasionally hang or crash. Learn to recover quickly by saving often and keeping track of your progress.
Save your work regularly and know exactly where it is stored. Keep a tidy, logical folder structure, and make copies of work that has taken a long time to achieve. GIS creates many files, and good organisation will save time and prevent data loss.
Explore the software rather than only following instructions. Be bold and click through menus, try tools, and experiment. You will learn faster by discovering features yourself. The practical exercises will expect you to find some things out for yourself.
Ask for help when needed. Support is available through Canvas video demos, classmates, demonstrators, and online resources. Coursework must be completed individually, but collaboration on problem-solving is encouraged.

title: Before you begin
text:
QGIS basics

Windows, panels, and toolbars
QGIS has two main windows: the Map Canvas and Print Layout. Within each window, you can open a number of toolbars (located along the top or left of each window by default) and panels (such as the Attribute Table to view and edit data linked to map features). You need to become familiar with opening and interacting with these main program elements.



The Map Canvas (top) and Print Layout (bottom) windows, with toolbars along the top (both windows) and left (Print Layout window only) of each window, and a series of panels which are either docked or floating (e.g. an Attributes Table (right)).




Layers
A layer is a dataset of a single type — vector or raster — loaded into QGIS from (often multiple associated) files saved on your network. Layers are combined to create maps or are processed to produce new layers. Layer order matters because higher layers can hide lower ones.


Projects
A QGIS project file (.qgz) stores references to your data and display settings, but doesn’t store the data itself. Projects therefore contain virtual links to all of the data files you’ve loaded, as well as instructions to the software as to how they should be displayed. This leads to three important considerations:

Moving QGIS projects. Copying or transferring a QGIS project from one computer to another would require copying the project file and all associated data layers in such a way as to maintain the relative file paths (the path to your data the QGIS project needs to load them). This is sometimes difficult to achieve. If you change your computer environment (e.g. from the University system to your laptop), it is often easier simply to copy all of the layer files and start a new project from scratch.
Moving or renaming data layers. Changing data layers (or the folders that contain them) will mean a QGIS project can no longer find them and so will fail to open them. It is possible to recover from this situation, but it’s easier to avoid in the first place. All data files on the master OneDrive will remain where they are. Make sure that all data files that you put on your OneDrive (or memory stick or laptop disk) are named sensibly and placed in an appropriate folder structure so that you don’t accidentally move, rename, or delete them. You will probably generate many hundreds of data files by downloading (e.g. from the internet), copying (e.g. from OneDrive), or creating layers in the course of GIS processing.
Working with temporary layers. When you create a new GIS layer (e.g. by performing a geoprocessing function on an existing layer), you are normally presented with the option of creating a temporary layer or saving the new layer to disk. Creating temporary layers is a quick way of exploring and confirming the output is what you wanted. However, these layers will no longer be available when you close the project unless you make them permanent. I recommend that use temporary layers for experimentation, and choose a permanent name, location, and data type for any layer that you will need later on.



Plugins
The basic installation of QGIS is adequate for most purposes, however the GIS practical exercises here go a bit beyond this basic functionality. Many QGIS add-ons have been developed through open source software development and made freely available through the Plugins interface. Plugins are installed in the user part of the computer storage so require no administrator privileges. You are encouraged to explore all available plugins. The practical exercises will explain when certain plugins need to be installed.

title: Before you begin
text:
Key considerations

Printing maps
Printed colours often look different from the colours you see on screen. If you need to print a map, always check that your chosen colours work well on paper. The best way to check this is to print a test copy, inspect it closely to make sure all map elements are clear and distinguishable, and adjust the colours if necessary. You may need to repeat this process a few times to get the result you want. Fortunately, all GEG276 coursework (and most assignments in other modules) is submitted online, so printing is rarely essential. Printers also usually cannot print right to the edges of the paper. If you plan to print directly from QGIS, leave at least a 0.5 cm margin around your map to avoid cutting off important details.


Using transparency
Transparency can help combine multiple layers without losing important details, but it can also make map colours inconsistent with the legend. Avoid partial transparency in final maps for coursework unless it adds essential meaning. Colours in the legend should match those in the map exactly.


GIS file types
There are several GIS file types. For raster data, I recommend saving them as GeoTIFF (.tif). For vector data (points, lines, or polygons), I recommend saving them as GeoPackage (.gpkg). You will likely come across Shapefiles as a format for storing vector data. This format has been around since the 90s and remains in wide use today. I recommend using GeoPackages instead for two reasons:

Efficient storage. A shapefile stores data as a number of files (between 3 and 16!) which have the same name but different extensions (.shp, .shx, .dbf…). If you rename or share a shapefile, you need to make sure that you rename all files and share all files for the new version to work correctly.
Flexible storage. A shapefile can only be a point, line, or polygon per file. A GeoPackage can store multiple data types.



GIS data sources
Use reputable sources for GIS data. In the UK, Ordnance Survey (OS) provides authoritative datasets, some of which are free via OS OpenData. As a Swansea University student, you can also access premium OS data through EDINA Digimap. Open data projects like OpenStreetMap offer free, continuously updated alternatives that are widely used in research and community projects. These data are continuously improving in quality and coverage and anyone can get involved in the project. I’ve chosen to use only Open Data sources for the practical exercises and project so that there are no restrictions on sharing data.


Customising the Map Canvas (advanced)
If you’re like me and you like a nice minimalist and clear interface to work with, one can customise the QGIS Map Canvas to a high degree. If you wish to do this, I recommend you explore the QGIS Documentation at your leisure here. But be careful! You may end up removing particular tools or menus that are essential for the completion of this course. So I recommend you only experiment with customisation after you’ve completed the course.

title: Before you begin
text:
Getting help
For general information, please refer to the GEG276 Canvas site. All documents associated with the course will be posted there, and I may use the Canvas Discussion Board to share extra information. If you don’t find what you’re looking for, feel free to email me. If I receive a query (the answer to which may be useful to all students), I will post a reply via email or the Discussion Board.
Software-specific problems can often be solved by Googling and asking AI. Typing QGIS and a description of your problem can often lead to a solution. Community-led sites like StackExchange are especially useful for getting help. The QGIS manual, QGIS Forum, and the main QGIS website are all valuable sources too.




Dikilitas, K., and I. N. Fructuoso. 2023. “Conceptual Framework for Flexible Learning Design: The Context of Flipped Classroom.” Learning Design for Flexible Education, nos. 2022-1-ES01-KA220-HED-000085250: 1–46. https://kudos.dfo.no/documents/77155/files/37244.pdf.


Graser, Anita, Tim Sutton, and Marco Bernasocchi. 2025. “The QGIS Project: Spatial Without Compromise.” Patterns 6 (7): 101265. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2025.101265.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.1 Starting up
To master QGIS, one must start with the basics. This exercise introduces the foundational skills that will underpin the development of your wind farm project and beyond - including your dissertation. Take your time, ask questions, and make sure you are confident with each step before moving on.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
Follow the steps here to access all the datasets you need for the practicals and the final project
Launch QGIS. This could be on a University computer, via a remote desktop, or on your own computer
From the menu bar, click Project → New. Find the shortcut icon to create a new project
Add your first vector layer in QGIS:

From the menu bar, click Layer → Add Layer → Add Vector Layer...
Click the Browse icon ()
Navigate to the folder where the data is stored, i.e. GEG276
Open the British_Isles_land_polygons folder and click on the corresponding .gpkg vector layer
Click Open → Add → Close. This dataset from the OpenStreetMap project consists of polygons representing the many islands making up the British Isles. Note the layer is now listed under the Layers panel. You can also drag-and-drop datasets from the browser straight into the Map Canvas

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.2 Navigation

Use the Map Navigation Toolbar to explore this dataset by panning and zooming







Try using the mouse scroll wheel as a shortcut
Make yourself familiar with navigating around the Map Canvas by losing yourself! Pan and zoom until you can’t see the British Isles layer anymore. Once lost, right-click on the layer in the Layers panel and click Zoom to Layer(s) to easily return to view that layer

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.3 Adjusting style properties

To adjust a layer’s symbology:

From the Layers panel, right-click on British_Isles_land_polygons and click Properties... → Symbology. A useful shortcut to Properties is to double-click the layer
Click Simple Fill and experiment with changing the layer symbology’s colours, styles, and widths. You have complete control over how vector layers appear. When designing a map, consider carefully how to choose an appropriate style for each layer
Click Apply → OK when you’ve finished editing the layer’s symbology

From the menu bar, click Project → Save
Use a sensible location and filing system on your OneDrive account to save your project and any data you generate. I recommend navigating to Documents and creating a GEG276 folder. You can create sub-folders within this too
Find the Save shortcut. Remember to save regularly from now on!

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.4 Measuring geospatial objects

Click the drop-down arrow next to the Measure icon to select the appropriate tool for measuring:
i The distance between the two furthest points on Great Britain (in miles)?

The approximate area of the Isle of Man (in square kilometres)








Use left-click to add points, and right-click to stop taking the length / area measurements



What is the distance between the two furthest points on Great Britain (in miles)?

What is the approximate area of the Isle of Man (in square kilometres)?




The distance between the two furthest points on Great Britain was 603 miles.
The approximate area of the Isle of Man was 571 square kilometres.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.5 Exploring the Attribute Table

From the Layers panel, right-click on British_Isles_land_polygons and click Open Attribute Table. An attribute table is a fundamental part of all GIS datasets. Each row of the table corresponds to a single feature (e.g. a polygon) of the vector layer, and each column, or attribute (of which there can be as many as is needed), records a property of the feature (e.g. name, area, circumference). This particular data layer has two attributes: fid (field identifier) and Area
Click the Dock Attribute Table icon () so that you can see both the Map Canvas and Attribute Table on screen at once
To understand how the attribute table corresponds with the vector layer:

Sort the attribute table according to each polygon’s area by clicking the Area column title. Repeated clicks will sort by ascending or descending the values
Click a row number to select the polygon to which it corresponds. The selected polygon in the Map Canvas has now been highlighted yellow
Click the Zoom map to the selected rows icon in the top-right corner () to zoom to the selected polygon in the Map Canvas








Repeat the step above to explore the ten largest islands of the British Isles



Can you name the seventh-largest island of the British Isles?

Lewis and HarrisIslayYnys Môn / AngleseyYnys Enlli / BardseySkye



The seventh-largest island of the British Isles is Ynys Môn / Anglesey.



You can also select features in the Map Canvas to identify their corresponding attributes in the attributes table:

Click the Select Features icon ()
Select (highlight in yellow) the Isle of Wight
In the attribute table, click the Move selection to top icon () to move the selected line of the table to the top
Read the area of the feature - which is in square metres - and convert it to square km (i.e. divide by 1,000,000)




What is the precise area of the Isle of Wight (in square kilometres)?



The precise area of the Isle of Wight was 382 square kilometres.



Click the Deselect features icon () to deselect the current selection. These functions will be very useful later on

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.6 Arranging layers

Add the Wales_Principal_Areas.gpkg layer in the UK_Boundaries folder to your project. This dataset consists of polygons representing the Principal Areas (otherwise known as counties) of Wales. Note this layer will also appear in the Layers panel
Adjust the style of this layer and explore its attribute table
Experiment with switching layer visibility on or off using the tick boxes in the Layers panel (). This becomes essential when managing multiple layers in a project
Change the order of the layers by dragging each upwards or downwards in the layer panel
Move Wales_Principle_Areas to the top of the Layers panel. Notice how the seaward political (Principal Area) boundary of Wales goes beyond the coastline (Land Polygons). This is because the physical land boundary is generally classified according to the mean high water mark, while administrative boundaries are normally classified according to the mean low water mark. That’s Geography!
To categorise the layer’s symbology:

Open the layer’s Symbology window
Use the drop-down menu to change the symbology source from Single Symbol to Categorized
Use the Value drop-down menu to select the attribute name
Click Classify → OK. How colourful!

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.7 Labelling layers

To label layers:

Select Wales_Principal_Areas layer in the Layers panel
From the menu bar, click Layer → Labeling. Find the shortcut to this window (hint - check out Properties...)
Use the drop-down menu to change the labelling source from No Labels to Single Labels
Change the Value drop-down menu to label the Wales Principle Area polygons according to their English or Welsh names

Experiment with modifying the labels by:

Changing the text style () e.g. style and size
Changing the label format () e.g. wrapping and orientation
Adding a text buffer ()
Changing the label placement ()
Playing around with other options. You are in complete control!
Have you saved your project recently?

Now that the Principal Areas have been labelled, zoom out. Notice how QGIS chooses to place and resize the labels so that they remain visible, but switches some of them off to avoid overlapping text. This is a fundamental part of map design and QGIS tries to optimize readability. You can control this behavior through the Labeling window and you are encouraged to experiment.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.8 Adding and filtering data

Add the vector layer Wales_operational_windfarms.gpkg to your project. These data are from the UK Renewable Energy Planning Database and represent the location of operational wind farms across Wales
Examine the attribute table
Adjust the layer’s style, noting that point data is represented in a different way to polygon data
Label the wind farms by their name or by their generation capacity
Add the vector layer gis_osm_roads_free_1.gpkg, which is in the folder British_Isles_geofabrik → wales, to your project. These data form part of the OpenStreetMap project and represent all roads in Wales. This is a large dataset and may take time to load and display
Once again, for this layer:

Examine the attribute table
Experiment with different styles for line data

There is a lot of data here! So let’s subset it. There are many ways to make subsets of data layers to select only the data you need or that you want to display. To filter the data universally:

Right-click on the roads layer and click Filter...
This tool allows you to easily see all the unique values contained in each field (or column) of the attribute table. Click fclass → All. You can now see all the unique classes of road in the vector layer
Under Provider Specific Filter Expression, type "fclass" IN ('primary', 'trunk', 'motorway'). Make sure of precise punctuation and spacing
Click OK. Your map should now only display roads classed as primary and secondary. A funnel icon () has also appeared next to the layer in name in the `Layers’ panel, to remind you a filter has been applied

Label the roads with the attribute ref (i.e. the road number). See how these labels are displayed as you zoom in and out of the map
To remove the filter:

Click the funnel icon () next to the roads layer
CLick Clear → OK

To filter the data by defining what is presented in the map:

Open the layer’s Symbology window
Use the Categorized option to categorise the road symbology according to the fclass attribute (remember to click Classify!)
Delete all the road classes except primary, trunk, and motorway using the Delete icon (). See if you can make this task easier for yourself by using the Shift and Ctrl keys…
Double-click the line symbol per category to choose a suitable symbology for these remaining roads (e.g. thick red for primary, very thick light blue for motorway)

Add the gis_osm_waterways_free_1.gpkg vector layer in the British_Isles_geofabrik → wales folders. What colour would be best for this layer?

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.9 Adding external data

Navigate to datamap.gov.wales
Search for “Wales Coast Path” and click on the link
Under Select spatial data format, choose OGC Geopackage and click Download
Move the downloaded file to your OneDrive
Add the layer to your project and explore it
Try searching for and downloading other GIS data files from datamap.gov.wales, geofabrik.de, or any another source. Searching for geospatial datasets should show you how easy it can be to find and download data from the internet. This will also provide inspiration for dissertation ideas, which is now on your horizon

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.10 Have you finished?

Congratulations! You’ve learned the basics of QGIS. Make sure that you’ve understood all the steps above. Repeat if necessary, and ask for help or advice from the demonstrators. You will need this knowledge in future exercises and for the assessments.







NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Create and manage a QGIS project by adding vector layers from various sources and using the navigation tools to pan, zoom, and return to a layer’s extent
Adjust the appearance of spatial data through symbology, layer ordering, and labelling to build a clear, readable map
Explore the attribute table to understand how features relate to their attributes, sorting records and selecting features reciprocally between table and map canvas
Measure and filter geographic data by obtaining lengths and areas, converting between units, and subsetting layers using filter expressions and categorised symbology
Appreciate how cartographic and administrative conventions shape spatial representation, from automated label placement to the way boundaries are drawn

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.1 Creating a print layout
Communication of geographical data and concepts through maps is a fundamental skill for spatial scientists. Creating maps requires both the ability to make them complete, correct and functional, and the flair to make them interesting and attractive. This exercise introduces the QGIS Print Layout window, and is how you generate the maps for your wind farm project.

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
Launch QGIS and create a new project
Add the British_Isles_land_polygons.gpkg, Wales_border.gpkg, and Wales_Principal_Areas.gpkg layers to your project (the latter two are in the UK_Boundaries folder)
Label the Principal Areas of Wales in Welsh or English
To create a Print Layout:

Click Project → New Print Layout... (and find the shortcuts to this window)
Give the print layout an appropriate title
Click Project → Layout Manager.... You can see here the Print Layout now saved within your project. You can create more than one print layout per project. Use this panel to access and organise layouts
Click Close

Change the page orientation and size, so it fits onto an A4 portrait document with space beneath to accommodate a caption:

Right‑click on the blank print layout
Click Page Properties...
Change Size to Custom
Reduce the map Height (e.g. to 270)
Change Orientation to Portrait

title: 2  Composing maps
section: 2.2 Adding and adjusting a map item
text:
2.2 Adding and adjusting a map item

Click Add Item → Add Map (look for the shortcut)
Draw a map onto the print layout. Map 1 should now appear under the Items tab







If necessary, adjust the map using the squares on the map boundaries so it fits more comfortably on the page
Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Set Scale to 1000000 (i.e. 1:1,000,000)
Use the Move item content () and Select/Move item () tools, and adjust the Scale value, to compose the map so that all of Wales is visible
Experiment with making fine adjustments to the scale by holding down the Ctrl key (windows) or Command key (mac) and scrolling the mouse wheel
Once you’re satisfied with the scaling, framing, and position, freeze the view in place by checking the box under the lock icon () for Map 1 in the Items panel
From the Map Canvas window, adjust layer styles:

Choose colours, border widths, and fonts that emphasise Wales and the difference between the outline of Wales (physical coast) and Principal Areas boundaries (non‑physical political construct)

Update the Print Layout to reflect your changes using one of these two options:

Click the Refresh icon () in the Print Layout window
Click the Update Map Preview icon () under Item Properties in the Map Canvas window

Click on the Item Properties tab and check Frame
Modify the frame’s Background colour appropriate for representing the ocean
You can modify the Layout and Item Properties of any item selected in the Item window. Note how the options under Layout and Item Properties tab update depending on what item you’ve selected. Remember that:

The order in which map items are listed is how they are also stacked on top of one another in the print layout
Some layer properties (e.g. layer order, style, labeling) are controlled in the Map Canvas

title: 2  Composing maps
section: 2.3 Adding a scale bar, north arrow, and grid
text:
2.3 Adding a scale bar, north arrow, and grid

From the Print Layout window, add a scale bar:

Click Add Item → Add Scale Bar
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the scale bar from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Adjust the scale bar’s properties, notably Style, Scalebar units, Segments, Frame, and Background

Add a north arrow:

Click Add Item → Add North Arrow
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the north arrow from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Under SVG Images, search arrow and choose a suitable north arrow
Adjust the north arrow’s properties, notably Fill color and Stroke color

Add a grid (aka graticule):

Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Expand Grids
Click Add a new grid ()
Click Grid 1 → Modify Grid...
Set CRS to EPSG:4326 - WGS 84
Set X and Y intervals to 1 degrees
Check Draw Coordinates
Adjust the grid’s properties, notably Grid type, Frame, and Draw Coordinates. Can you adjust the labels for readability, soften the gridlines, and reduce unnecessary trailing zeros?

You may find that some of the map items, notably the coordinates, are now beyond the edge of the page. These will be lost when the map is exported! In these cases, you will need to adjust the map size periodically as you experiment with how to best arrange map items and the caption (see Section 2.2). Check how using guides can aid you in aligning map items perfectly on the page (see FAQ).

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.4 Adding labels and a legend

Add a map title label:

Click Add Item → Add Label
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the label from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Adjust the label’s properties, notably Main Properties, Font, Rotation, Frame, and Background

Add a legend:

Click Add Item → Add Legend
Drag and drop on the map to place it (you can move it later)
Select the legend from the Items panel
Click the Item Properties tab
Uncheck Auto update to enable modifications to the legend
Experiment with the legend toolbar icons () to improve the legend
Adjust the legend’s properties, notably Arrangement, Fonts and Text Formatting, Columns, Symbol, Spacing, Frame, and Background

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.5 Adding raster data

Add your first raster layer in QGIS:

From the menu bar in the Map Canvas, click Layer → Add Layer → Add Raster Layer...
Click the Browse icon () and navigate to the folder where the data is stored, i.e. GEG276
Open the Wales_mean_windspeed folder and click on any of the .tif raster layers
Click Open → Add → Close

Change the raster layer’s colour ramp:

Open the layer’s Properties... → Symbology
Use the Render type drop-down menu to select Singleband pseudocolor
Under Color ramp, select an appropriate colour ramp for the data (or pick one you just really like!)
Click OK

Adjust the order and modify the properties of the Wales Principal Areas and windspeed layers so both are visible at the same time. Hint: modifying Fill or Transparency properties may do nicely, but be careful to not break the link between the map and legend colours
In the Print Layout window, select Map 1 and click Update Map Preview under the Item Properties tab
If the colour scale for the raster layer does not appear in the legend, add it
Experiment with improving the aesthetics of the updated legend
Select Map 1 from the Items panel
Under Item Properties, check the Lock layers and Lock styles for layers to prevent further changes to the map. Uncheck if you need to make edits

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.6 Adding an inset map

Add a second map to provide an inset showing the British Isles (see Section 2.2)
Modify this second map to create an effective inset map that provides geographic context for the main map:

Adjust the inset map so the whole of the British Isles are visible
Modify which layers should be displayed by turning layer visibility on and off or changing the layer order
Modify the layers’ symbology








TipScale matters



Place emphasis on only a few, simply presented layers that are useful at this scale. Aim to be minimalist to avoid cluttering the map. Note: because your map of Wales (Map 1) is locked, it’s not affected by changes in layer visibility or symbology being made for the inset. Herein lies the power of locking layers.



Add an extent indicator on your main map to connect it to the inset map:

Select your inset map (Map 2) from the Items panel
Under Item Properties, expand the Overviews tab
Click Add a new overview ()
Click Overview 1
Set the Map frame to your main map (Map 1)
Adjust the Frame style to draw a hollow rectangle with a thick line, to easily show the main map’s extent
Experiment further, especially with Fill color, Stroke color, and Join style

Projects can get rapidly out of control when multiple layers are used to build a map. It’s important to remove redundant layers and label items appropriately. E.g. try renaming Map 1 to Main, and Map 2 to Inset. This will help when you need to revisit and adjust your maps

title: 2  Composing maps
text:
2.7 Exporting your map

Ensure both maps have Lock layers checked so that your formatting is captured in the exported maps
To export your map as an image:

Click Layout → Export as Image...
Select a suitable location to save the map
Set the image format to PNG (.png)
Click Save
Set Export resolution to 300 dpi (300 dpi is suitable for viewing on a screen, 600 dpi is better for printing)
Click Save

Congratulations - you’ve created your first QGIS map assignment. Now make any revisions (including the map height) to be able to submit the best Map 1 that you can!







NoteLearning outcomes



By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Create a scaled print layout in QGIS, setting page size and orientation and framing a map item at a fixed scale
Add the essential furniture of a complete map — scale bar, north arrow, graticule, title, caption, and legend — and adjust their properties for clarity
Integrate raster and vector data in a single layout, applying pseudocolour rendering and managing layer order and transparency so both remain legible
Construct an inset map using locked layers and an overview frame to place the main map in its wider geographic context
Export a print-ready map to PDF with appropriate vector, text, and compression settings, and appreciate how locking layers preserves scale integrity

title: Cwestiynau Cyffredin
text:
Dyma rai o’r problemau cyffredin sy’n codi yn ystod y cwrs hwn a sut i’w datrys.






NoteNid yw fy map allforiedig yn edrych fel oedden i’n ddisgwyl





Pan fyddwch chi’n argraffu neu allforio map o QGIS, nid yw’r feddalwedd yn anfon yn union be sy’n weladwy yn y Print Layout i’r argraffydd. Mae QGIS yn cyfeirio at osodiadau’r eitemau map i ddiffinio beth sy’n cael ei argraffu a sut y dylai ymddangos. Os gwnaethoch chi newidiadau i un o’r eitemau map ers i chi adnewyddu’r sgrin ddiwethaf, efallai na fydd y map yn cael ei argraffu fel oeddech chi’n ddisgwyl. Bydd gwneud haen yn weladwy mewn un eitem map yn ei gwneud yn weladwy’n awtomatig (wrth argraffu neu adnewyddu) mewn un arall oni bai eich bod chi’n dewis cloi’r haenau.
I wneud yn siŵr eich bod chi’n argraffu neu’n allforio’n union yr hyn oeddech chi’n bwriadu, ar gyfer pob eitem map:

Cyfansoddwch yr eitem map gan ddefnyddio’r haenau sydd eu hangen arnoch a’u priodweddau fel y dewiswch
Ticiwch y bocs lock layers for map item sydd o dan y tab Item Properties
Adnewyddwch y sgrin (Golygfa > Adnewyddu) i wneud yn siŵr bod popeth yn edrych fel y ddymunwch
Dim ond wedyn y dylech chi argraffu neu allforio










NoteNid yw fy attributes table yn edrych fel dwi’n disgwyl





Mae’n debyg bod golwg yr attributes table wedi newid o ‘table’ i ‘form’ trwy gamgymeriad. I’w newid yn ôl, cliciwch yr eicon Switch to table view ()









NoteMae’r ffenestr “Handle Bad Layers” yn ymddangos pan dwi’n agor prosiect





Os, pan fyddwch chi’n agor prosiect sy’n bodoli eisoes, ydych chi’n cael neges yn dweud ‘Handle Bad Layers’, yna ni all eich prosiect QGIS gysylltu â rhai neu’r holl haenau data rydych chi wedi’u hagor o’r blaen. Gall hyn ddigwydd os byddwch chi’n symud neu’n dileu ffeiliau data sy’n rhan o’ch prosiect yn anfwriadol. Yr unig ffordd i adfer yw rhoi pethau yn ôl fel yr oeddent, neu ailagor y ‘Bad Layers’.
Rheswm posibl arall am ‘Bad Layers’ yw bod OneDrive wedi methu cysylltu’n gywir â’ch cyfrifiadur pan wnaethoch chi fewngofnodi. Yr ateb gorau yw allgofnodi ac mewngofnodi eto.









NoteRwy’n cael y gwall “One or more input features have invalid geometry”





‘Invalid geometry’ yw pan fydd haen fector yn torri, fel pan fydd ffin polygon yn croesi ei hun neu pan fydd gan linell hyd sero. Gall geometregau annilys ymddangos wrth drin haenau e.e. clipio ffyrdd i’ch deilsen map.
I ddatrys ‘invalid geometries’:

Gwnewch yn siŵr bod y Processing Toolbox yn weladwy drwy glicio ar yr eicon cocsen ()
Chwiliwch am fix geometries
Dwbl-gliciwch ar Fix geometries
O dan y cwymplen Input layer, dewiswch yr haen fector tramgwyddus
Cliciwch Run → Close

Bydd haen newydd yn cael ei chreu, sy’n edrych yn union yr un fath â’r haen wreiddiol, gyda’r geometregau toredig wedi’u datrys. Gallwch nawr fwrw ymlaen â’ch llif gwaith gwreiddiol.









NoteMae fy newislen “Processing” ar goll





Mae’r ddewislen ‘Processing’ yn ategyn QGIS, felly mae’n debygol bod yr ategyn ar goll yn eich prosiect.
I’w ychwanegu yn ôl i mewn:

Cliciwch ar Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins...
Chwiliwch am processing
Ticiwch y blwch ger Processing
Cliciwch Close

Dylai’r ddewislen ‘Processing’ nawr fod yn weladwy.









NoteNi chadwyd fy ngwaith





Y tri rheswm mwyaf tebygol yw:

Fe wnaethoch chi allgofnodi o’ch cyfrifiadur cyn i OneDrive gael amser i gysoni ffeiliau’n gywir (h.y. symud eich data o’r cyfrifiadur i’r cwmwl). Gwnewch yn siŵr bob amser bod tic bach wrth ymyl eich ffeil yn y porwr i gadarnhau bod y ffeil wedi’i gysoni’n gywir.
Fe wnaethoch chi gadw’r data yn ‘lleol’ (h.y. ar y cyfrifiadur) yn hytrach nag ar eich OneDrive. Efallai byddwch chi’n gallu adfer eich ffeiliau os byddwch chi’n dychwelyd i’r union gyfrifiadur roeddech chi’n ei ddefnyddio, ac yna’n cadw’r data ar eich OneDrive. Ond, mae cyfrifiaduron y Brifysgol yn cael eu dileu bob dydd Gwener - felly byddwch yn gyflym!
Rydych chi wedi cadw’r data ar eich OneDrive, ond allwch chi ddim cofio ble. Ceisiwch ddod o hyd i’r ffeiliau o dan yr eicon ‘Recent’ ar eich porwr, yna cadwch nhw yn rhywle mwy synhwyrol.










NoteSut alla i drefnu eitemau map yn berffaith ar y print layout?





Defnyddiwch ‘guides’. Mae’r rhain yn caniatáu ichi snapio eitemau map (e.e. ymyl map) ar y llinell, gan alinio popeth yn berffaith.
I ychwanegu tywyslinellau:

Cliciwch y tab Guides, neu cliciwch View → Show Guides os nad ydyn nhw’n weladwy
Cliciwch yr eicon Add new guide ()
Gosodwch bellter y tywyslinell, a fydd mewn mm o’r brig (tywyslinellau llorweddol) neu o’r chwith (tywyslinellau fertigol)










NoteMae un o fy mhaneli ar goll, sut alla i ei gael yn ôl?





Os oes panel neu far offer ar goll:

Cliciwch View → Panels or Toolbars
Dewiswch y panel/bar offer perthnasol
